ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the bottom is a common lower wire, and the output voltage Uo is marked on the right, with its positive terminal at the upper-right output node and its negative terminal at the bottom common node. In the middle left there is a 6 V power supply, marked with the upper terminal “−” and the lower terminal “+”; its upper terminal is connected to the upper-right output node through a 5 kΩ resistor R. In the right branch, D2 is located between the output node and the upper terminal of a 3 V power supply; this 3 V power supply is also marked with the upper terminal “−” and the lower terminal “+”, and the lower terminal is connected to the bottom common node. On the left side there is also a diode D1 connected between the upper node and the bottom common node. Reasoning: According to the specified method, take the bottom common wire as 0 V. Since the lower terminal of the 6 V power supply is positive and connected to 0 V, the potential of the upper terminal node is -6 V; since the lower terminal of the 3 V power supply is positive and connected to 0 V, the potential of the upper terminal node is -3 V. The resistor R will pull the output node toward -6 V, while the D2 branch is connected to the -3 V reference point, so first assume D2 conducts. The forward voltage drop of the silicon diode is 0.6 V. According to the conducting polarity of D2 in the figure, the output node is 0.6 V lower than the -3 V node, so Uo = -3 - 0.6 = -3.6 V. Check: When the output node is -3.6 V, D2 forward conduction holds; D1, relative to the bottom 0 V node, does not satisfy the forward bias of its conducting direction, so it does not conduct. The assumption is consistent.

raw_record.question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) are silicon diodes with a forward voltage of 0.6 V. The voltage \(U_o\) is ________ V.

method.method_draft: Take the bottom rail as 0 V. From the image, the node at the top of the 6 V source is -6 V and the node at the top of the 3 V source is -3 V. First suppose D2 conducts because the resistor tends to pull the output node toward -6 V while the D2 branch is tied to -3 V. Apply the 0.6 V forward drop across D2 in the polarity indicated by its symbol, giving the output node 0.6 V below the -3 V reference: Uo = -3 - 0.6 = -3.6 V. Then verify consistency: at -3.6 V, D2 is forward biased, while D1 connected to the 0 V bottom rail is not forward biased in its conducting direction, so the assumed state is valid.
